title: Fatality inquiry starts in the shooting death of 17-year-old Cyrus Green in 2011
article: When Const. Jack Redlick got out of his car in an alley across the street from Rexall Place, he could see the suspect police had been chasing carrying a red, aluminum baseball bat in his right hand.
He drew his firearm, yelling at the man -- later identified as 17-year-old Cyrus Green -- to drop the bat. But the teen looked at him with anger, said Redlick, and started sprinting towards him.
"He yells in pure anger "You're going to have to shoot me,'" said Redlick during the first day of a fatality inquiry into the fatal shooting of Green in February 2011.
According to Redlick, Green also had a knife and raised it to his shoulder as if he was holding a spear. Redlick again ordered the suspect to stop. He was now only about 10 feet away.
Thinking he was too close, Redlick fired three shots at Green. He has no mental thought of even putting his finger on the trigger.
"He didn't stop running. He took like two more steps. I thought I missed him -- that he would stab me in the throat," said an emotional Redlick, adding Green soon fell down at his feet.
When officers flipped him over, Redlick said Green looked up at him with anger and stated, "Shoot me again."
"That's something I won't ever forget," Redlick said.
The court was told about the string of events leading up to Green's death that cold winter night.

At the time, Redlick was working neighbourhood foot patrol in the Boyle Street/McCauley area when he and another beat officer heard a call on the radio about a personal robbery at the Coliseum LRT. Two people were taken into custody, but a third person had fled from police.

The officer on the radio was chasing the suspect on foot. He sounded panicked, said Redlick, noting the suspect had a bat and a knife. He had also challenged the officer, prompting Redlick to respond to the scene.

Following the gunfire, the injured teen was taken to hospital where he passed away from multiple gunshot wounds to the chest. Toxicology results showed he was just over the legal alcohol limit for driving and also had marijuana in his system.
The incident was turned over to the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), which later ruled the officer's actions were justified and he was acting in self defence.
Green's family wiped away tears as they listened to Redlick, whose credibility was challenged by one of the lawyers. His mother, Carol Green, doesn't believe the officer's story.

"What happened to my son shouldn't have happened. My son was a very caring, loving boy," said Carol outside of court. She's since launched an $85,000 lawsuit against Redlick and former Police Chief Mike Boyd, citing she has suffered grief and loss of the guidance, care and companionship of her son.
"Every day goes by, you see somebody that looks like him.it's so hard."
The inquiry continues Tuesday and is meant to find recommendations that would prevent similar deaths from occurring.
